content.text: {"relation": "DIVERGENT", "consensus_summary": "All three blind responses converge on lamp oil symbolizing the Holy Spirit — the Spirit's indwelling presence, anointing, and empowering that fuels the believer's light (Matt 25:1-13; Zech 4; Exod 27:20; 1 Sam 16:13; Acts 10:38). Secondary readings are widely acknowledged: readiness/vigilance without a specific allegorical referent (common in academic exegesis), good works or charity (patristic/Catholic), genuine faith or grace, and rarely the Word of God or joy. Two of three responses affirm a settled popular consensus on the Holy Spirit; the third notes stratification but still names the Spirit as the dominant association.", "book_summary": "The book defines lamp oil not as the Holy Spirit itself but as Spirit-taught truth and correction that is received, retained, and worked into proven obedience — a 'pressed' inward store produced by accepting reproof (Ps 141:5; Prov 27:5-6) and buying truth (Prov 23:23), which the wise keep in reserve (Prov 21:20). Light is then that obedience made visible as an example to others (Matt 5:16). The entry explicitly flags the common view (Holy Spirit as anointing/empowering) as the position it departs from.", "rationale": "The book's own common-view note concedes that the standard interpretation is the Holy Spirit, and the book replaces that referent with something else: the internalized product of receiving correction and truth, worked into obedience. While it retains a Spirit connection (Ezek 36:27; Zech 4:6) and overlaps loosely with the 'good works' and 'word/truth' alternatives noted as minority readings in the consensus, its central claim — oil as received reproof/instruction stored as proven obedience, grounded in Ps 141:5, Prov 21:20, 23:23, and 27:5-9 — is not represented in any blind response and displaces the dominant 'oil = the Spirit himself' identification rather than refining it. The distinctive correction/reproof axis (Ps 141:5's 'let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil') appears in none of the consensus responses. Because a recognizable consensus exists and the book contradicts/displaces it with a materially different referent, DIVERGENT fits better than NOVEL or REFINED.", "citation_support": "PARTIAL", "strongest_objection": "One could argue for REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: the book still treats the Spirit as the source ('Spirit-taught,' Ezek 36:27, Zech 4:6), and the consensus responses themselves note minority readings of oil as good works, truth/word, or authentic inward life — so the book could be seen as a sharpened synthesis of acknowledged alternatives (Spirit-produced obedience) rather than a genuine displacement of the common view. Additionally, Ps 141:5 explicitly calls reproof 'an excellent oil,' giving the book a direct textual anchor that arguably strengthens its citation support beyond 'partial.'", "confidence": "high"}
